prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator with time-reversal symmetry, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B050 as my preferred prize, unchanged from round 1, and the exchange has made me more rather than less sure of the structure of the case. What I value is the pairing of a sharp prediction with a measurable quantity: Kane and Mele showed that spin-orbit coupling can give a time-reversal-protected insulating state, classified by a Z2 invariant, with conducting edge channels, and Molenkamp's group then measured the predicted quantised edge conductance in HgTe/CdTe wells. Nobody in the first round disputes that the physics holds. Eriksson, Olsson and Pearce all describe roughly two decades of independent confirmation in transport and ARPES, and even the members who prefer something else (Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig) say they would not block it. I did not reach this position by counting support. I moved to it from inflation because a discovery where the idea and the measurement are both in hand is stronger, for this prize, than a larger idea whose mechanism is still open. On the chair's question about the 2016 prize, I would draft the citation around the time-reversal-invariant Z2 state and its edge transport. Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz were honoured for topological phase transitions and for topological order in quantum Hall-type and one-dimensional systems, and a state protected by time-reversal symmetry with no net magnetic field was not part of that work. I would anchor the citation on the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect and leave the three-dimensional generalisation out of the wording.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real and I have not talked myself out of it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe proposal that told Molenkamp where to look, and Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, and Hasan's group built the three-dimensional picture. Under a limit of three people, the prize cannot honour all of them. Johansson calls the omission a decisive theory contribution left out, and Lindroth calls it a defect in the prize itself. I understand both and cannot say they are wrong. My view is that the prize can still be defended if the citation is written narrowly: Kane and Mele for the prediction of the effect and the Z2 state, and Molenkamp for its first observation, with no claim to the HgTe design recipe or to the three-dimensional materials. The honest cost is that the committee must record that choice openly. A second residual risk is that a topology-themed prize ten years after 2016 will look repetitive to some in the Academy. I would still prefer to defend that criticism than to give up the experimental half. A theory-only Kane-Mele prize is the fallback if the committee decides the HgTe observation cannot be credited without BHZ, but I would regard that as a weaker prize, because the confirmation is what makes the case compelling.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B050 as a conceptual reorganisation of band-insulator physics, regards B051 as a superb refinement, and says that if the BHZ omission proves indefensible he would move to B051 or B002.
responses.response: We agree on the substance and on the 2016 distinction, and your answer to Pearce on that point is the one I would use in committee. I disagree with one thing. Your reading of B051 as a refinement is not how its supporters see it, and I do not think it is how I should argue it either. Kroll and Lindroth make a case that the magic-wavelength condition is a new principle, and I would not want B050 to win by being described as the only conceptual candidate. For me it wins because both halves of the claim are tested. I would also ask you the chair's question directly. If a BHZ credit replaced Mele, would the Kane-Mele prediction still be fairly represented? I think not, since Mele's name belongs with the Z2 state, so I would not trade him out. Replacing Molenkamp with BHZ is the choice I find harder to accept, because it would turn a theory-plus-experiment prize into a theory-only one.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether the 2D quantum spin Hall effect or the 3D topological insulators should anchor the citation, and says she would keep Molenkamp because the quantised edge conductance is what makes this a discovery.
responses.response: I agree with your reasoning on Molenkamp and I hold the same position. The question you and I both raised in round 1 now has an answer I can state: the 2D effect should anchor the citation. It is the prediction that Molenkamp's measurement directly tests, whereas the 3D materials were identified later by ARPES and by a different set of people, namely Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan, none of whom are credited. If the committee wrote the citation around three-dimensional topological insulators, the credited names would be wrong for it. I would go one step further than your round-1 position. We should not let the generic wording in your citation, which says topological insulators without qualification, stand into the final text, because that wording invites the 3D reading. I would keep my own wording about the quantum spin Hall state and the HgTe quantum wells.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B051 but names B050 as his first alternative, argues that the magic-wavelength lattice is a different principle from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion work, and says B050's credit has a real defect that the clock entry does not share.
responses.response: Your point about attribution is the strongest argument against my position, and I accept that Katori and Ye cover both the idea and the record realisation in a way that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp do not. I also agree with you and with Lindroth that the pending SI redefinition should not decide this. A prize recognises the discovery, not the metrological schedule. Where we still differ is the criterion the chair asked about. You said B050 opened an organising principle while the clock opened a new level of accuracy. I accept that framing, and I think a new organising principle with a messy credit still ranks above a very good advance with a clean credit, provided the citation is narrow enough to be true. I would ask you to state whether you would accept B050 if the citation were limited to the quantum spin Hall effect and its observation. I would accept B051 as a good outcome, drafted narrowly around the lattice clock, and that is why it remains my first alternative.

responses.point: Johansson calls the BHZ omission a decisive theory contribution left out and is unsure about the distance from 2016, but says B050 is a credible alternative he would not block.
responses.response: I take your objection on BHZ seriously, and I would rather answer it than ignore it. Their paper identified the HgTe/CdTe system and the critical thickness at which the inverted band structure appears, so it is a materials route to the effect and not the effect itself. Kane and Mele predicted the state and the Z2 classification a year earlier, and Molenkamp's group is the one that made and measured the devices. That is why I think the omission is a limit of the three-person rule and not a reason to say the achievement is wrongly attributed. I do not claim this is comfortable. On 2016 I would invite you to name what you think is shared. If it is the word topological, I would say the physics is different. If you think the shared element is the Chern-number classification, then I would like to hear why time-reversal symmetry and Z2 do not separate the two. On your own entry, B015 shares the same Wineland overlap problem in a harder form, and I do not see that you have resolved it.

responses.point: Pearce moved from B009 to B050, says safety should not be mistaken for the best science, and wants the citation kept to the quantum spin Hall prediction and the HgTe observation to keep the 2016 overlap narrow.
responses.response: I agree with your citation advice, and my wording above follows it. Your remark that B050 is the safe consensus choice and that safety is not the same as best science is one I should answer for myself. I do not hold B050 because it is safe. I hold it because I think it satisfies the criterion of a discovery with a decisive measurement better than any other entry that has the breadth to be taken seriously. You asked in round 1 whether I would back B050 if the credit could not be resolved, and your question to me was fair. The answer is that I would still choose it over B003 and B009, but the fallback is B051, not a reduced B050. I would also note that you and I started from candidates the room did not support, you from IceCube and I from inflation, and we ended in the same place for scientific reasons, not because we wanted the room to agree.

responses.point: Lindroth prefers B051 for its clean two-name credit and many-body-limited systematics, calls the BHZ omission a defect in the prize itself, and would not oppose B050 if the committee can settle the credit.
responses.response: Your answer to my round-1 question about Ye is helpful: the control of collective and density-dependent shifts, which showed that the many-atom advantage survives, is more than accuracy engineering, and I would defend that in committee. I still think B050 has the stronger case, because its credit problem is bounded and can be handled by wording. The issue I would press is how you would handle the same criticism of B051. You rightly said that Lemonde, Lisdat and the JILA line are left out, and that this is true of every candidate. If so, the uncredited-contributor objection cannot be a decisive point against B050 and a minor point for B051. I would accept that the defect is real in both, and the question is which prize is the more important discovery. I do not claim this settles it. You say your first place reflects your specialty, and I think that is a candid statement.

uncertainties: Whether the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang can be defended under the three-person limit, or whether the committee will judge that it makes the experimental half of the citation untenable.

Whether the Academy will see a second topology-themed prize within ten years as distinct enough, given that the 2016 distinction rests on time-reversal symmetry and Z2 classification, which is a judgement and not a fact I can prove.

Whether wording the citation around the 2D quantum spin Hall effect is the right anchor, since the three-dimensional topological insulators arguably had the larger materials impact and are not covered by the credited names.
I am working from my own recollection of priority and credit in this field, which is outside my own research area, and I have not verified details such as the dates of the BHZ and Kane-Mele papers.
statement.conflict_note: No change. My documented connections are David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theoretical-physics group, and none of them is a credited person on any shortlisted entry. My field proximity is to inflation (B003), which I ranked first at opening and have discounted; B003 is no longer among my alternatives. As the chair noted, I have no stated conflict for B050 or B051, and I do not think any recusal is needed on my part.
